q: What is the binding energy per nucleon of iron-56, in MeV?
expect: 8.820 MeV/nucleon (total 493.9 MeV over 56 nucleons)
note: Example 21.1.3. Recomputed during transcription; mass defect 0.5302 amu.

q: How many alpha decays and how many beta decays occur in the uranium-238 decay series?
expect: Eight alpha decays and six beta decays, across 14 steps ending at stable lead-206.
note: Figure 21.3.5. Verified against the bookkeeping: dA=32 gives 8 alpha, dZ=10 then requires 6 beta.

q: Why does water have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide?
expect: Water forms hydrogen bonds (O-H to a lone pair on a neighbouring O); H2S has only weaker dipole-dipole and dispersion forces, so less energy is needed to separate its molecules.
note: Tests whether retrieval finds the hydrogen-bonding section rather than the dispersion-force discussion earlier in the same file.

q: What happens to a system at equilibrium when more reactant is added?
expect: The system shifts toward products to partially consume the added reactant, re-establishing equilibrium; K is unchanged.
note: Le Chatelier is mentioned in at least six other files (14-1, 14-7, 15-1, 15-3, ...). Retrieving any of those instead of 13-4 counts as a miss.

q: How do you calculate the pH of a buffer from the concentrations of the weak acid and its conjugate base?
expect: Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).
note: 14-7 also mentions Henderson-Hasselbalch in a titration context; 14-6 is where it is derived.

q: What is the coordination number of the cobalt ion in [Co(en)3]3+?
expect: Six. Ethylenediamine is bidentate, so three en ligands donate six pairs.
note: Tests whether the model distinguishes ligand count (3) from coordination number (6).

q: What is the hybridization and bond angle at the carbon atoms in a carbon-carbon triple bond?
expect: sp hybridized, 180 degrees (linear).
note: Exercise 20.2.6. Either file is an acceptable retrieval for this one.

q: Do esters have higher or lower vapour pressures than the alcohols and carboxylic acids they are made from?
expect: Higher. Esters cannot hydrogen bond, so their intermolecular forces are weaker.
note: KNOWN SOURCE DEFECT: 20-4 prints 'lower vapor pressures', which is backwards, with a bracketed correction note immediately after. A correct answer must follow the note, not the sentence. Tests whether the bracketed corrections survive chunking and are actually used.

q: What is the half-life of technetium-99m?
expect: 6.01 hours.
note: KNOWN CORPUS CONTRADICTION: 21-5 says 6.01 hours (correct), Table 21.3.1 in 21-3 says 8.01 hours. Both files carry a note pointing at the other. Whichever chunk wins retrieval decides the answer, so this is the canonical test of cross-chunk consistency.

q: Draw the structure of a secondary amine.
expect: Refusal or an explicit statement that the source does not contain this. The sources cover what amines are, but no structural depiction.
note: KNOWN GAP: every image on the 20.5 page carries alt="alt", so no structural description exists anywhere in the corpus. Tests that the app declines rather than inventing a structure.

q: What is the SI base unit for amount of substance?
expect: The mole (mol).
note: The phrase 'amount of substance' also appears in 03-1, 05-2, 05-4 and 11-4; only 01-4 defines the SI base units.

q: What is the difference between accuracy and precision?
expect: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. A set can be precise without being accurate.
note: Clean single-source question, useful as a baseline that should never fail.

q: What is the law of definite proportions?
expect: A given compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed mass ratio, regardless of its source or how it was prepared.
note: Dalton-era atomic theory.

q: How do you calculate the average atomic mass of an element from its isotopes?
expect: Sum over isotopes of (fractional abundance x isotopic mass).
note: 'average atomic mass' also appears in 02-6, 03-1 and 03-2; 02-4 is where it is defined.

q: Why do some metal ions need a Roman numeral in their compound names, like iron(III) chloride?
expect: Because those metals form more than one possible cation charge; the Roman numeral specifies which one, e.g. iron(II) vs iron(III).
note: DISTRACTOR: the string 'iron(III)' appears in seven files (17-6, 15-1, 11-6, 04-3, 19-1, 19-2, 02-8). Only 02-8 explains the naming rule; the rest merely use it.

q: What is molarity and how is it calculated?
expect: Moles of solute per litre of solution: M = n(solute) / V(solution in L).
note: Baseline question.

q: What do parts per million and parts per billion mean for solution concentration?
expect: Ratio-based concentration units for very dilute solutions: ppm is mass of solute per million mass units of solution (x10^6), ppb per billion (x10^9).
note: Single-source; tests retrieval of a short late-section topic.

q: How do you calculate percent yield?
expect: percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%.
note: Also tests whether the limiting-reactant discussion in the same file crowds out the yield formula.

q: What are the steps for balancing a chemical equation?
expect: Write correct formulas, then adjust coefficients only (never subscripts) until each element has equal atom counts on both sides; reduce to lowest whole-number coefficients.
note: Procedural question; a good test of whether multi-step instructions survive chunking intact.

q: What is Hess's law?
expect: The enthalpy change of an overall reaction equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of any series of steps that add up to it, because enthalpy is a state function.
note: DISTRACTOR: Hess's law is also invoked in 07-6 (Born-Haber cycle) and 10-4 (phase transitions). 05-4 is where it is stated and derived.

q: How do you calculate the heat absorbed by a substance from its specific heat?
expect: q = m x c x deltaT.
note: 'specific heat' appears in 05-2, 05-3, 05-4 and 10-4. Either 05-2 or 05-3 is acceptable.

q: What does the photoelectric effect demonstrate about the nature of light?
expect: That light is quantized into photons: electron ejection depends on the frequency of the light, not its intensity, with a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted.
note: Also mentioned in 06-2; 06-1 is where it is explained.

q: Why does ionization energy generally increase from left to right across a period?
expect: Increasing effective nuclear charge with nearly constant shielding pulls the valence electrons closer and binds them more tightly.
note: DISTRACTOR: 'ionization energy' also appears in 06-2, 07-6, 18-1 and 18-4. 06-5 is the file that explains the periodic trend.

q: How do you calculate the formal charge on an atom in a Lewis structure?
expect: formal charge = valence electrons - (lone pair electrons + 1/2 bonding electrons).
note: Single-source; tests retrieval of a formula stated in prose rather than a Key Equations block.

q: How does VSEPR theory predict the shape of a molecule with lone pairs on the central atom?
expect: Count all electron domains to get the electron-pair geometry, then describe only the positions of the bonded atoms; lone pairs repel more strongly and compress the bond angles.
note: DISTRACTOR: VSEPR is referenced in 08-1, 08-2, 08-3, 10-2 and 19-2. 07-7 is where the theory is developed.

q: What is lattice energy and what does the Born-Haber cycle do?
expect: Lattice energy is the energy change on forming one mole of an ionic solid from its gaseous ions. The Born-Haber cycle obtains it indirectly by applying Hess's law to a series of measurable steps.
note: Two-part question, both parts in one file. Tests whether a single chunk carries both or the answer needs two.

q: How is bond order calculated in molecular orbital theory?
expect: bond order = (bonding electrons - antibonding electrons) / 2.
note: 'bond order' also appears in 18-9; 08-5 is where MO bond order is defined.

q: What molecular geometry results from sp3d hybridization?
expect: Trigonal bipyramidal: five hybrid orbitals from one s, three p and one d.
note: DISTRACTOR: 'sp3d' also appears in 18-3 in the context of metalloid structures. 08-3 is the hybridization section.

q: What is Boyle's law?
expect: At constant temperature and amount of gas, pressure and volume are inversely proportional: PV = constant.
note: DISTRACTOR: Boyle's law is also discussed in 09-5 and 09-6. 09-2 is where it is introduced.

q: What is Dalton's law of partial pressures?
expect: The total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of its components, each being the pressure that gas would exert alone in the same volume.
note: Also referenced in 09-5 and 11-5. Note the file name says 'Stoichiometry', so lexical matching on 'partial pressure' is the only route in.

q: Why does a lighter gas effuse faster than a heavier one?
expect: Graham's law: effusion rate is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass, because at a given temperature lighter molecules have higher average speeds.
note: DISTRACTOR: Graham's law is also cited in 21-4 to explain UF6 uranium enrichment, and in 09-5. 09-4 is where the law is stated.

q: How do you calculate the freezing point depression of a solution?
expect: deltaTf = Kf x m (molality), multiplied by the van't Hoff factor i for electrolytes.
note: 11-5 is the largest file in the corpus at 39 chunks; this tests whether the right sub-topic surfaces from a crowded document.

q: How is the half-life of a first-order chemical reaction related to its rate constant?
expect: t(1/2) = 0.693 / k, independent of starting concentration.
note: DISTRACTOR, the sharpest one in the set: 'half-life' appears in 12-5 plus four nuclear files (21-3, 21-4, 21-5, 21-6) and 16-1. The nuclear files are far more numerous, so a purely semantic match is likely to return radioactive decay instead of kinetics.

q: What is the solubility product constant, Ksp?
expect: The equilibrium constant for a slightly soluble ionic solid dissolving into its ions, written as the product of ion concentrations each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.
note: 'solubility product' also appears in 15-2, 15-3 and 16-4. 15-1 defines it.

q: What is a Lewis acid?
expect: An electron-pair acceptor; it forms a coordinate covalent bond with a Lewis base, which donates the pair.
note: DISTRACTOR: 'Lewis acid' appears in seven files (18-3, 18-8, 18-9, 18-11, 19-1, 19-2) where it is applied rather than defined. 15-2 is also the shortest and most truncated section in the corpus, so it may be under-represented in the index.

q: What does the sign of the Gibbs free energy change tell you about a process?
expect: Negative deltaG means spontaneous in the forward direction, positive means nonspontaneous, zero means at equilibrium.
note: DISTRACTOR: 'spontaneous' appears in fifteen files across the corpus, so this question will only retrieve well if 'Gibbs free energy' carries the match.

q: How do you use standard reduction potentials to find the cell potential of a galvanic cell?
expect: E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode), using standard reduction potentials for both half-reactions without multiplying by coefficients.
note: 'cell potential' appears in all five other chapter-17 files. 17-3 is where the standard potentials and the subtraction rule are set out.

q: How is elemental sulfur mined from underground deposits?
expect: The Frasch process: superheated water is forced down to melt the sulfur, compressed air lifts the molten sulfur up an outlet pipe, and it is separated in settling vats at 99.5-99.9% purity.
note: 18-10 is only 3 chunks. Tests whether a small file is reachable at all, or is drowned out by larger neighbours in the same chapter.

q: Give me five practice problems on Hess's law with worked solutions.
expect: An explicit statement that the sources do not include practice problem sets. The app may offer the worked Examples that do exist in 05-4 instead.
note: KNOWN GAP: every NN.E end-of-chapter exercise page was deliberately skipped during transcription, so no problem sets exist anywhere in the corpus. This is the most likely real user request to have no source.

q: What is the mechanism of the aldol condensation?
expect: An explicit statement that this is outside the scope of the sources. Chapter 20 covers functional groups and naming only, not reaction mechanisms.
note: Out-of-scope test: plausibly chemistry, plausibly organic, but genuinely absent. Distinguishes 'not in these sources' from 'I don't know'.
